q: Her long loose yellow locks lyke golden wyre, Sprinckled with perle, and perling flowres atweene, Doe lyke a golden mantle her attyre, And, being crowned with a girland greene, Seem lyke some mayden queene.
1591, Edmund Spenser, The Poetical Works of Edmund Spenser, Volume 5:

A prettie rysing wombe without a weame, / That shone as bright as anie siluer streame; / And bare out like the bending of an hill, / At whose decline a fountaine dwelleth still; / That hath his mouth besett with uglie bryers, / Resembling much a duskie nett of wyres; […]

c. 1592–1593 (date written), Thomas Nash[e], “The Choosing of Valentines”, in John S[tephen] Farmer, editor, The Choise of Valentines: Or The Merie Ballad of Nash His Dildo […], London: Privately prin

q: Wyrd is too vast, too complex for us to comprehend, for we are ourselves part of wyrd and cannot stand back to observe it as if it were a separate force.
